about: Daventre (Deventer) on the IJssel, 793-1066: one port of the region rhine_frisia. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/daventre.md and the spine; a draft in the game's own file, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what could not be checked; 'invented' marks ordinary people and small things the sources do not give.

ports.summary: A wooden church on a river dune, a row of houses on a sand ridge and a bank where boats lie, on the east side of the IJssel where the king's land ends and the Saxons' begins. The road from the Rhine to the Weser crosses the river here, so every May the host and its carts cross too. A merchant comes to sell to the army and the church, to buy heath iron, eels, horses and Saxon honey, and to hear what is happening in the east before anyone downriver knows.
ports.seasons: After Easter the count's men buy up grain, horses and salt meat for the host, and prices on the bank go up until the army has marched. At summer's end the river is low enough to wade; after Martinmas it rises, a second channel runs round the north-east and the place is an island until spring, with ice in a hard winter. Lebuin's feast is the morrow of Martinmas.

history.text: Lebuin (Liafwin), an English priest, came to Utrecht, and was sent from there to the IJssel.
About this year Lebuin's wooden church was built on the river dune; Saxons burned it and it was built again.
history.source: dossier 2: Canon van Deventer, 'Lebuinus'; Vita Lebuini antiqua. The year of the first burning is not in the Life (770 and 772 are both printed)

history.text: About 773 to 775 Lebuin died here. The church was burned again after his death, and the Saxons looked three days for his body and did not find it.
history.source: dossier 6 and 7: Vita Lebuini antiqua; de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebuin

history.text: About 775 to 777 Liudger, sent by Alberic of Utrecht, built the church a third time, found the grave under the south wall he had just raised, and moved the foundations so that the grave lay inside.
history.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.13-15 (ed. Diekamp 1881); dossier 2 and 7

history.text: The Saxons and the East Frisians rose again and burned churches; the road east from the IJssel was not safe.
About 802 to 803 the law of the Franks of 'Amor' was written down in 48 chapters: a Frankish man's wergild 600 solidi, a freeman's 200. 'Amor' is usually read as Hamaland, the land about this river.
About this year the clergy of Utrecht fled the Northmen; for some sixty-five years the bishops of Utrecht kept a house here.
history.source: dossier 5: nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geschiedenis_van_Deventer. Whether Bishop Hunger himself lived here is unclear

history.text: On 20 June Charles the Bald confirmed to the abbey of Saint-Bertin seven manses 'in Daventre portu'.
history.source: Guérard, Cartulaire de l'abbaye de Saint-Bertin (1840), p. 124-125

history.text: Late in the year the Northmen burned the port 'called Taventeri in the Frisian tongue, where Saint Liobomus rests', and killed many.
history.source: Annales Fuldenses 882 (ed. Kurze 1891, p. 99); our rendering

history.text: Before 890 an earth wall was finished round the place, over a layer of burning 20 cm thick: sods, probably a palisade, 1.9 km long.
King Zwentibold ruled on the king's toll at Deventer and Tiel in favour of the church of Utrecht, whose men were to have the freedom they had had at Dorestad.
history.source: Oorkondenboek van het Sticht Utrecht I no. 88, 24 June 896; Regesta Imperii I no. 1964, not seen (?). Another report makes it the church's tenth of the toll

history.text: On 29 November Bishop Radboud died at Ootmarsum and was buried here, in the north part of the church.
About this year Bishop Balderic took the see back to Utrecht.
In 952, 956 and 960 Otto I gave the king's property here to Saint Maurice's at Magdeburg: a court, two farmsteads and some thirty dwellings. The charters call the place urbs or civitas.
history.source: dossier 2: Rijksdienst voor de Monumentenzorg, Toelichting beschermd stadsgezicht Deventer (1986)

history.text: About this year the first pennies were struck here, reading ODDO REX and DAVNER/A in three lines after the pennies of Cologne. In the spring of 990 the oak was felled for a flat river barge that later went into the quay.
history.source: dossier 2 and 4: Canon van Deventer, 'Deventer munt'; Künker, Otto III pfennig; Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, MaSS, Deventer 1

history.text: After this year the king's mint struck the Hand type, which Countess Adela of Hamaland had struck first, with the English king's Hand on one side and Deventer's cross on the other.
history.source: 'Munten van gravin Adela', Jaarboek voor Munt- en Penningkunde 67 (1980) 213-215

history.text: About this year Bishop Bernold built the stone basilica: three aisles, columns, transepts, a westwork and a crypt.
history.source: dossier 2: Canon van Deventer, 'Lebuinuskerk'; L. Bosman in Madoc 1993

history.text: Henry III gave Deventer, with toll, mint and justice, and the county in Hamaland to the bishop of Utrecht.
history.source: dossier 4 and 5: Canon van Deventer, 'Deventer munt' and 'Lebuinuskerk'; nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernold

eras.text: The border in wartime. A wooden church, fishers, a few traders and a smith; every spring the count's men, carts and horse lines for the host that goes into Saxony, and every autumn hostages coming back west over the ferry. Saxon converts and Frankish soldiers stand at the same Mass.

The war is over and the place is quiet: a church town on a minor river, under the law of the Franks of 'Amor'. The Saxons across the border have bishops of their own now, and the road east carries wine, quernstones and pots instead of spears.

The bishop of Utrecht's people are here in exile and Dorestad's merchants follow as their river fails. New plots are pegged out along the bank; a timber revetment holds it; an abbey in the far west holds seven manses 'in the port'.
Burned by the Northmen late in 882. For some years the bank is charcoal and new timber, and everyone who has stayed carries sods for a wall nearly two kilometres round.
A walled port and a bishop's seat. The king's toll is taken on the bank, the church's men go free of it as they did at Dorestad, and Bishop Radboud writes verses in a house by Lebuin's church.

The bishop has gone home to Utrecht. What is left is the king's: a court, two farmsteads, some thirty dwellings inside the wall, given piece by piece to Magdeburg. A stone church stands where the wooden one was. Barges of Ardennes oak work the river.

A mint town. Deventer and Tiel strike the pennies of these lands, and most of them go north and east to pay for furs and wax. Old barges are broken up to face the quay. About 1040 Bishop Bernold's basilica rises over the saint.
The bishop's town: toll, mint and court are his by the emperor's gift, twenty canons and a provost sing in the basilica, and a bishop's palace stands against its north side.

sites.name: The bank below the church
sites.see: A sloping bank of sand and trodden mud, boats drawn up bow first and two barges moored to stakes; behind them the sand ridge with its row of thatched houses, and to the right the wooden church on its dune. Across the brown river lies the Worp, flat, green and empty. It smells of tar, wet rope and smoked eel; in May there are carts on it from end to end.
sites.source: dossier 1 and 2: boats lay along the line of today's Polstraat, the quay until the 12th century; the oldest of three timber revetments there is 9th-century, so in 793 it is a bare bank (?)

sites.name: Lebuin's church
sites.see: A plank church with a thatched roof on a river dune, the third on the spot; the posts of the south wall are newer than the rest and stand a stride further out. Inside it is dark, one lamp over a stone slab in the floor on the south side; Franks stand north of the slab and Saxons south. A hand bell, wet thatch and tallow.
sites.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.13-15; dossier 2. Wooden until 882, stone under Bishop Balderic in the 10th century. Who stood where at Mass is invented, from the spine's hook (cross_and_grove)

sites.name: Saint Lebuin's basilica
sites.see: Grey tuff walls higher than anything else on the river: three aisles on round columns, two transepts, a square westwork toward the bank. Steps go down into a crypt where lamps burn before the relics of Lebuin and Marchelm. Canons sing the hours; masons are still working on the north side, where the bishop's palace is going up.
sites.source: dossier 2: Canon van Deventer, 'Lebuinuskerk'; Madoc 1993. The chapter of twenty canons and a provost is mid 11th century

sites.name: The churchyard
sites.see: Open trodden ground between the church and the houses, graves marked with posts along the church side. After Mass and on feast days people set out what they have on cloths and cart tails: eels in baskets, honey in crocks, a horse held by its halter, pots from the Rhine. Saxon and Frankish are spoken across the same cloth, slowly.
sites.source: The square by the church is still the Grote Kerkhof, the great churchyard (dossier 6). An early market is only supposed (dossier 2), so that it was held here is the game's (?)

sites.name: The crossing to the Worp
sites.see: A flat ferry barge on a pole and two oars, nosed into the east bank beside a post with a horn hanging on it. The far side is low grass with a cart track going west toward the heath, and upstream of it, small against the trees, the roof of Lebuin's chapel at Wilp. In late summer sandbars show and the ferryman wades the horses over.
sites.source: dossier 1: the high ground on both sides comes closest here, the road to Westphalia crosses, the river was easily fordable, the Worp was never built on, Lebuin's chapel stood at Wilp on the west bank. The ferry itself is invented; capitularies allow a toll only where a ferry or bridge gives help (npc_roles_793.json, ferryman)

sites.name: The host's ground
sites.see: A sandy field on the ridge north of the houses, grazed bare. From Easter to midsummer it holds horse lines, ox carts wheel to wheel, stacked sacks under hides and a count's man with a wax tablet at a trestle. Smoke of cooking fires, dung, and a smith's boy going from cart to cart with a bucket of nails.
sites.source: spine thread saxon_end, hook for daventre; chains/house_debt.md step 8; chronicle_793.json 794-autumn-sintfeld, 795-summer-bardowick-campaign, 797-summer-ships-into-saxony. The field is invented

sites.name: The forge on the bank
sites.see: An open-sided shed at the south end of the bank, its thatch black above the hearth. Bars of dark iron from the heath lie stacked by the door like firewood; kegs of rivets stand in a row. Hammer, bellows, the hiss of the trough, and charcoal smoke that follows you down the bank.
sites.source: invented, with the card harbour.chain_house_new_ship.s04_iron: iron was smelted on the Veluwe west of the IJssel (goods_793.json bar_iron; nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veluwe)

sites.name: Hathugard's ale-house
sites.see: The last house on the ridge toward the bank, a low door, a bush on a pole above it. Two benches along a hearth in the middle of the floor, a brewing tub in the corner, cattle heard through the wattle at the far end in the Saxon way. The woman at the tub looks at every stranger's hands and boots before she looks at his face.
sites.source: invented; the Saxon woman who asks every boat about a hostage son is the spine's hook (saxon_end). Cattle under the same roof: Design/content/peoples/saxon.md 2

sites.name: The houses on the ridge
sites.see: A single row of timber houses along the top of a sand ridge, end on to the river, each with a yard, a pit for storage and a boat path down to the bank. From 863 pegs and strings mark new plots between them, and the ground is being raised with sods against the floods.
sites.source: dossier 2: a 7th- or 8th-century building 4 m under today's ground between Engestraat, Broederenstraat and Lange Bisschopstraat, lying as the streets still lie; the ground raised later against floods. The plots after 863 are the spine's hook (dorestad_falls)

sites.name: The weirs at the brook mouth
sites.see: South of the bank a brook comes in under alders, and across its mouth run two fences of stakes and wattle with basket traps in the gaps. A logboat is tied to the last stake. Eels hang smoking on a rack over a slow fire; herons stand in the shallows and wait their turn.
sites.source: dossier 1: the Hunneper Aa (later Schipbeek) joins on the south side; 'a small fishing and trading settlement'. The weirs are invented; Ælfric's fisherman takes eels, pike and salmon (npc_roles_793.json)

sites.name: The Heest
sites.see: A second dune south-east of the church, steep where the river and the brook have cut it, covered in low beech scrub. Nobody lives on it. A path goes up that nobody admits to using, and at the top, in a hollow, there are things on the ground: a crock, a twist of rags, the ash of a small fire.
sites.source: dossier 1: the Berg, called Heest after its beech scrub, with no sign of early building. The offerings are invented, after the vows at trees and groves and the idols of rags forbidden in the Saxon capitulary and the Indiculus superstitionum (Design/content/peoples/saxon.md 4)

sites.name: The barge slip
sites.see: A cut in the bank north of the houses where a flat barge lies on rollers, half planked: oak boards pegged with wood, moss driven into the seams. Beside it an old barge is being broken up plank by plank, and the good timber goes down to the water to hold the bank.
sites.source: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, MaSS, Deventer 1 (spring 990: flat-bottomed, oak, moss caulking, wooden pegs), Deventer 2 (about 1035), Deventer 3 (after about 913), all reused in the quay. A slip here in 793 is assumed (?)

sites.name: The bishop's house
sites.see: A timber hall with a fenced yard a little way from the church, better roofed than its neighbours and no bigger. Clerks sit in the doorway for the light with wax tablets and a chest of charters behind them. A swallow's nest is stuck under the eave over the door, and nobody is allowed to knock it down.
sites.source: dossier 2: a substitute court of the Utrecht bishops from about 857 to about 920; where it stood is not known. The swallow is from Radboud's poem on a swallow (nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radboud_van_Utrecht); the nest is invented

sites.name: The earth wall
sites.see: A bank of earth and cut sods as high as a house, a palisade of split oak along the top and a wet ditch at its foot, running in a long curve from the river round the houses and back to the river. Where it is being dug you can see a black band a hand deep under the grass: what was here before.
sites.source: dossier 2: Canon van Deventer, 'Verdedigingswal' (raised after 882 over a burn layer 20 cm thick; 1.9 km; finished before 890; later 7.5 m high and 23 m broad); Rijksmonument 525006

sites.name: The king's toll
sites.see: A post with a beam across the head of the bank and a lean-to beside it, where a toll man looks into every boat before a sack comes out of her. A church's man shows a token and walks through. From 1046 the toll man is the bishop's and looks the same.
sites.source: dossier 4: the toll the king's by 896 (Zwentibold; van der Aa dates it 890); toll, mint and justice to the bishop in 1046. Before 896 a toll here is not recorded, so the site opens then

sites.name: The mint
sites.see: A strong house inside the wall with one door and a man at it. Inside, a hearth, a block with an iron die set in it and a second die in the moneyer's fist; silver sheet is cut with shears into rounds and each is struck with one blow. New pennies lie in a wooden bowl, pale, with a cross on them.
sites.source: dossier 2 and 4: mint from about 990, first site unknown; ODDO REX / DAVNER/A; from 1046 the bishop's. No moneyer is named

people.name: Brunger
people.trait: Strong, loyal to the boat, slow to speak and slower to forgive; said the baptismal vow because the law is baptism or death.
people.want: To find his younger brother, given as a hostage when their district submitted in 785 and sent to a lord in the south.
people.fear: The king's men, and a priest asking what he ate in Lent.
people.voice: Plain Saxon words, and not many at a time; a proverb when he is pleased, silence when he is not.
people.looks: Late twenties, tall and heavy in the shoulder, long fair hair, a moustache and no beard; an undyed tunic, a long knife (a seax) across his belly.
knows: the road east to the Weser and which villages on it were burned
the IJssel at low water, bar by bar
Old Saxon, and how much a Saxon understands of Frisian
who on the bank sells to the host and who hides his grain

ties.note: the same person
his mother; he winters at her hearth
the ferryman carried the family over when their village burned
the priest counts who fasts; Brunger does not like being counted
the count led the levy that burned his village; the count does not know him
the boy reads; Brunger thinks reading is how his brother will be found
has hauled oak down the bank for the wright, who pays in rivets and silence
his younger brother, for whom he has asked along the whole river
a woman of his own district on the Weser, who knew his mother's name before he gave it
hers is the one house on the Rhine where he sits with his back to the door
the priest who read the vow over a boatload of Weser men in 785, himself and his brother among them
the one person on the Rhine he will sit beside; she knows why
a king's steward; that is enough. The man does not know him and would not remember the village
she pours for him without asking where he is from; he has never broken a bench of hers
she lodges Saxons who would not be moved over the Elbe; he is welcome there for their sake

lines.greet: You came up the river, which is good. My mother has a bench for you and questions for you, and you should answer the questions first.
lines.greet_again: The boat sits level, so somebody loaded her right this time.
rumour: The count's men are buying oats again. When Franks buy oats in spring, Saxons bury their honey.
A man from the Weser crossed last night with no cloak and no name. I did not see him, and neither did you.
lines.saying: A baptised wolf still knows the wood.
lines.lent: Do not ask me what I ate in Lent, because the priest asks enough for both of you.
lines.friend: I said the vow with a spear at my back, but nobody makes me pull your oar.
lines.farewell: Go well. If you hear of a Saxon hostage called Brunric anywhere south, bring the word home like silver.

people.source: invented; the spine's cast.crew.brunger with the same facts. The hostages and the vow are chronicle_793.json and texts_793.json saxon_vow. The brother's name Brunric (Brun- + -ric, the family stem) is this file's and should be made to agree with whoever writes Mogontia

people.name: Hathugard
people.trait: Brews the best ale on the bank and asks every boat the same question; has forgiven nobody and says so pleasantly.
people.want: Word of her younger son, counted off as a hostage in 785 when he was thirteen and led west over the ferry.
people.fear: That he is alive, a Frank in everything but his hair, and would not know her; or that he is dead and nobody thought her worth telling.
people.voice: Asks first, pours second. Flat plain Saxon, with a short laugh at her own expense.
people.looks: About fifty, tall and straight, grey-fair hair under a linen cloth, a brown dress pinned with one bronze brooch, sleeves rolled, a wooden ladle in her hand.
knows: every boat that has lain here since 785 and where it had been
which of the count's men pay and which take
what Saxons across the border will give for wine, pots and quernstones
the old vows, which she no longer says aloud

ties.note: her elder son
he carried her son west in 785 and has told her so; she drinks with him anyway
the priest buried her husband in the churchyard without asking what he had believed
the smith's custom is the host; hers is everyone the host frightens
her elder son, the mate of the boat
his levy burned her house on the Weser; she has served his men ale since, at a fair price
a cousin by marriage who brews on the bank at Noviomagus; they send each other yeast and bad news
the palace clerk can read the old tally of the hostages of 785 (invented); she has never got near him
passes his word to those left at home, and theirs back to him
a Saxon woman on the Rhine; boatmen carry a word between them twice a year
an ale-wife far up the river who asks her question for her of every hauler
her younger son, counted off as a hostage in 785; she does not yet know where he is

lines.greet: Sit down, and hear me before you drink. If you go up the Rhine, look for a Saxon boy who was given as a hostage in the year the dukes bowed. He would be a man now.
lines.greet_again: So it is you again, for the same bench and the same question. Did you hear of any Saxon hostage in a lord's house south of Colonia?
rumour: The host eats this bank bare every May. Sell them salt pork and they pay in the king's new pennies, on the days when they pay at all.
The ferryman counts who crosses and I count who comes back, and his number is the bigger one.
lines.saying: Ale sours in time, but grief keeps.
lines.winter: After Martinmas the river goes round us on both sides, and we are an island with ale on it, so you could winter in worse places.
lines.friend: So it is Mogontia. You have given me a town to hate by name, which is more than the priest ever gave me.
lines.farewell: Go with God, since he is the one we have now, and ask at every landing.

people.source: invented; the spine's hook for daventre in the thread saxon_end. Name of two attested Saxon parts, Hathu- and -gard (Design/content/peoples/saxon.md 7). Brewing as women's work: npc_roles_793.json, alewife

people.name: Liudbod
people.trait: Patient and practical: a schoolboy of Utrecht who carried planks when the church was built the third time and has kept it standing since.
people.want: A bell, a psalter the damp has not eaten, and Saxons who come to Mass without a soldier behind them.
people.fear: A fourth fire; and what his own flock leaves on the Heest at night.
people.voice: Mild, dry Frisian. Says every date by its feast. Never raises his voice and rarely needs to.
people.looks: Mid thirties in 793, small and thin, tonsured, a patched grey cloak over a priest's long tunic, wooden shoes, a ring of keys and a hand bell at his belt.
knows: where Lebuin lies and how the grave was found
who of his flock was baptised by choice and who by the king's law
the feast days and fasts, and what may be sold on them
what Liudger is doing and where he is this year
letters: he reads Latin and will read a text for a guest

ties.note: Liudger was the young master he carried planks for about 776; he still writes to him
sends him word of the border and lodges him when he rides through to the western Saxons
the church is a daughter of Utrecht; the bishop is his lord and owes him a bell
writes to Saint Martin's each Easter for books and gets a blessing
buried her husband and asked no questions; she has not thanked him
suspects him of meat in Lent and of worse on the Heest
the smith mends the church's hinges for a Mass said for his son

lines.greet: God keep you. The Franks stand north of the grave and the Saxons south of it, but you may stand where you like, since you are a Frisian and fit nowhere.
lines.greet_again: You are back again, and whole. I said a psalm for the boat, though I will not say which one, in case it was the wrong one.
rumour: Liudger has been driven off the Frisian shore this year. He will be back, because he has been burned out of better places than that.
The soldiers hear Mass with their swords on. When I asked the count about it, he said that the Saxons hear it with their memories on.
lines.saying: This church has burned twice and stands a third time. Wood is patient, and so was he.
lines.feast: Lebuin's day is the morrow of Martinmas. Come then: the goose is still fat and even the Saxons sing.
lines.friend: I was a boy carrying planks when Liudger found the grave, under the wall he had just raised. He said nothing for a while. Then he moved the wall.
lines.farewell: Go safely, and if you pass Traiectum, tell the bishop that the bell rope is ready and lacks only the bell.

people.source: invented: no priest of the place is named before 1066 (dossier 8). Name of two attested Frisian parts, Liud- and -bod. The finding of the grave and the moved wall: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.15, told in our own words

people.name: Einbert
people.trait: Proud of heath iron and of the king, in that order; judges a man by his hands.
people.want: A steady buyer for rivets and tools who is not the host, and his son back from the carts.
people.fear: The king's men asking every smith who buys blades, and where the blades go.
people.voice: Loud, because of the hammer; a Frank who says 'our king' twice in a breath.
people.looks: About forty, broad, short brown hair singed at the front, a long moustache, a leather apron over a bare chest, burn scars on both forearms, tongs in his fist.
knows: the price of bar iron and rivets here and at Dorestad
what the host orders each spring, so where it is going
the law of 779: no mail coat leaves the realm
who smelts on the heath and who cuts the charcoal

ties.note: works for the count's stores every spring and is paid at Michaelmas, usually
the count's steward keeps the tally of what the forge has been paid in advance
hinges for a Mass
she will not serve the count's men first; he thinks that is bad for trade
the ferry brings his iron over from the heath; they settle at Martinmas
the keeper of the palace larder at Noviomagus orders his hooks, knives and nails here, and pays late
a marsh smith who takes his heath iron by the Almere boats, and pays a keg behind (?)

lines.greet: Mind the sparks! This is heath iron, smelted across the river, and the best this side of Colonia. I have rivets and nails, and an axe head cooling.
lines.greet_again: So your rivets held, then, and now you must come and see what is on the anvil.
rumour: The host wants nails, axe heads and spear ferrules by the hundred, by Pentecost. I sleep when they march.
The king's men ask every smith who buys blades and where they go. You should buy rivets, because nobody was ever hanged for rivets.
lines.saying: Cold iron and a Saxon: neither bends because you shout.
lines.friend: My boy went east with the count's carts, and he is fourteen. When the host comes back over the ferry, count the carters for me.
lines.farewell: Keep her tight, because tar hides a bad rivet only until the sea finds it.

people.source: invented; he is the smith of the card harbour.chain_house_new_ship.s04_iron ('the smith on the IJssel bank'). Name of two attested Frankish parts, Ein- and -bert. Herstal 779 on mail coats: the spine's thread swords_north

people.name: Thancric
people.trait: Counts everything that crosses and takes no side out loud; has carried saints' men, hostages and armies over the same water for the same fare.
people.want: To keep the crossing in his own hands, which means the count must go on finding him useful.
people.fear: Being put on oath to say who crossed by night.
people.voice: Slow, and all numbers, days and depths. Tells you a thing once.
people.looks: Mid forties, lean and brown, grey hair loose to the shoulder in the Saxon way, a straw hat, bare legs wet to the knee, a long ash pole worn pale where his hands go.
knows: who crossed, when, and with how many horses
where the hostages of 785 were led and whose men led them
the river: the bars, the wading place at summer's end, the winter channel round the north-east
the way to Wilp and the track over the heath

ties.note: he ferried her younger son west with the hostages and told her so himself
taught him the river
carries his iron; settles at Martinmas
the count's host crosses on his barge each May, at the count's price
has carried him and his horse many times and never been asked his faith twice
the ferryman of the Batua crossing says IJssel men cannot read brown water; Thancric says the Waal is a ditch with opinions
handed the hostages of 785 to the palace's men on the west bank; the clerk there keeps such tallies (invented)

lines.greet: A penny for a man, two for a horse, nothing for news if you bring some.
lines.greet_again: It is you. The river is a hand lower than when you left, so keep to the east bank past the brook.
rumour: Forty carts for the host since Easter, and eleven horses for one lord alone. Somebody on the Weser will sleep badly.
In the year the dukes bowed I carried the hostages west. Boys mostly, roped in fours. A clerk at the palace at Noviomagus has the tally.
lines.saying: The river asks nobody's faith, and it drowns both kinds.
lines.low_water: By summer's end a tall man can wade here. The host knows it, and so do the Saxons.
lines.friend: I do not see who crosses at night, because I am old and I sleep. Remember that I said so, if anyone asks you.
lines.farewell: Go on with you, since the water will tell you more than I will.

people.source: invented. Name of two attested Saxon parts, Thanc- and -ric. The straw hat: Widukind III.2 (Design/content/peoples/saxon.md 2). A toll only where a ferry or bridge gives help: capitularies of 805 and 809 (npc_roles_793.json)

people.name: Thiadlef
people.trait: A Dorestad man without a Dorestad: careful, sour, and the first on the bank with a measuring string.
people.want: The old house's name on a new bank, and here the freedom from toll that the church's men had at home.
people.fear: That the Northmen follow the trade up the IJssel as they followed it up the Rhine.
people.voice: Dry Frisian. Measures everything against Dorestad and finds it short.
people.looks: Thirties in 863, grey by 882; spare, clean-shaven, a good blue Frisian cloak gone thin at the hem, a knotted measuring string round his wrist and a folding balance in a case at his belt.
knows: which Dorestad houses went to Tiel, which to Utrecht and which came here
what a plot on the bank costs and who sells it
the bishop's steward and what he wants for a favour
prices on the Rhine and the Waal, a month old

ties.note: says Thiadbod of the dam head was his grandfather's father; nobody is left to say otherwise (invented)
paid Rorik's toll at Dorestad for thirteen years and reckons he is owed a river for it
Rorik's man on the dam heads took his toll and, in the end, his jetty
the count's son the Northmen held in the palace in the winter of 880; Thiadlef carried part of his mother's ransom down the river (invented; the ransom is Regino 881)
did not live to see him; his sons hold the plot of Radboud
a cousin at Diusburg, burned out the year after he was
brings the margrave word of what moves on the IJssel

lines.greet: You are from Dorestat, by your boat. Nobody is from Dorestat now, and we are all from here. Mind the pegs as you come, because that string is my street.
lines.greet_again: So you are still afloat. The bank is longer since you left, by two more plots, both of them taken by men I knew on the dam heads.
rumour: An abbey far in the west holds seven farms in this port, under the king's seal. Monks know where silver is going before merchants do.
lines.saying: At Dorestat the river left us, and here it only floods us, which is an improvement.
lines.before_882: The Northmen wintered in the palace at Noviomagus. From there to here is three days, for men who row for pleasure.
lines.after_882: They burned it to the ground, and the ground itself a hand deep. Now the bishop wants a wall, so here I am carrying sods at my age.
lines.friend: My grandfather's storehouse stood on a dam head a ship's length long, and I have a string and four pegs. You should buy the plot beside mine.
lines.farewell: Good trade to you, and if you pass the old place, do not tell me what grows on it.

people.source: invented; the spine's hook for daventre in the thread dorestad_falls ('new plots on the IJssel, old Dorestad names on them'). That Dorestad's merchants came here is 'probable' only (dossier 4). Name of two attested Frisian parts, Thiad- and -lef. Saint-Bertin's seven manses: Guérard 1840, p. 124-125

people.name: Radboud
people.trait: A scholar bred at a king's court who would rather write verses than judge tolls; of the heathen king Radbod's line through his mother, and gently amused by it.
people.want: To see Saint Martin's at Utrecht again; until then, Lebuin's feast well kept and his Life well written.
people.fear: Dying in exile with his church still in ashes downriver.
people.voice: Courteous and light. A learned man who talks about birds and weather so as not to talk about charters.
people.looks: About fifty in 900, thin, tonsured, a pale lined face, a plain dark cloak over a bishop's white tunic, a plain staff, ink on the first two fingers of his right hand.
knows: King Zwentibold's ruling of 896 and what it frees the church's men from
the Life of Lebuin, which he has written about himself
the quarrel with the count of Hamaland
Latin: he will read a text, and let a trusted guest copy one
who is king this year, which in Lotharingia is worth asking

ties.note: Balderic follows him in 918 and takes the see home about 920
Thiadlef's sons hold their plot of him and bring him news of the river
Eberhard's house holds the county in Hamaland: his kinsman Meginhard is count 898 to about 915, and Radboud is said to have taken their quarrel to the pope about 914 (?)
never met him: but it is Northmen of that kind who hold the river mouths and keep him from his church

lines.greet: You are welcome. I am bishop of Traiectum, which is why you find me here, because the Northmen have my church and I have Lebuin's. Sit down.
lines.greet_again: Here is the merchant. Tell me what the river is doing, because my clerks only tell me what the charters are doing.
rumour: King Zwentibold gave our men here the freedom they had at Dorestat. A dead town's rights, carried upriver like relics.
The count of this land and I do not agree. One of us must walk to Rome about it. I am the one with the shoes.
lines.saying: My mother's kin had a king who would not be baptised. God is patient, and has a sense of order.
lines.feast: On the morrow of Martinmas we keep Lebuin, who was an Englishman, buried among Saxons, and minded now by a Frank with Frisian blood. The church is like that.
lines.friend: A swallow nests over my door each spring. I have written her some verses. She is the only one of my flock who comes back on time.
lines.farewell: Go with God. The swallow goes south without paying toll, but you will have to pay yours.

people.source: nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radboud_van_Utrecht and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radbod_of_Utrecht (dossier 3): bishop 899/900 to 917, living at Deventer, of King Radbod's line through his mother, bred at Charles the Bald's court, wrote on Lebuin and a poem on a swallow, died at Ootmarsum 29 November 917 and was buried here. His birth year (about 850) and the walk to Rome about 914 are (?). His words are invented

people.name: Hrotmar
people.trait: Exact, unhurried, privately delighted at how far his pennies travel.
people.want: Good silver coming in and nobody copying his dies badly.
people.fear: Light coin laid at his door: a false moneyer loses the hand he struck with.
people.voice: Precise. Gives weights before he gives opinions, and seldom gets to the opinions.
people.looks: About thirty in 990, stocky, fair hair cut short, clean-shaven, a leather apron, a hammer with a short handle, a small folding balance on a cord round his neck.
knows: what a penny of Deventer weighs this year, and Tiel's and Cologne's
what foreign and old silver changes for, and the king's share
that his coin goes north and east for furs and wax and does not come back
Countess Adela's penny with the English king's Hand on it

ties.note: the Utrecht merchant says Deventer pennies are light and takes them anyway; Hrotmar has offered to weigh him one
her husband strikes a lighter penny on the Ems; she calls Hrotmar one of the heavy-penny men, and he takes it as praise
never met: but the silver England pays the fleets comes up this river as Hand pennies, and he melts it
another Tiel man who says his pennies are light and takes them anyway
the Count Palatine's steward takes his pennies without weighing them

lines.greet: Silver goes in and pennies come out, with the king's share off the top. Old coin, foreign coin and broken rings are all one to the fire.
lines.greet_again: Your last silver was honest. I mention it because it is rarer than you think.
rumour: The countess struck a penny with the English king's Hand on it and our cross behind. Now the king's mint copies her. Nobody copies a bad coin.
My pennies go north for furs and wax and I never see one twice. Somewhere a Northman is cutting the king's name in half.
lines.saying: A penny has two faces and no opinions.
lines.law: A false moneyer loses the hand he struck with, so I count my fingers every Easter.
lines.friend: Bring me English Hand pennies and I give you weight for weight, less a little. The die-cutter likes one to look at.
lines.farewell: Weigh what they give you, as I do.

people.source: invented: no moneyer of Deventer is named (dossier 3 and 8). Name of two attested Saxon parts, Hrot- and -mar. The coins: Canon van Deventer, 'Deventer munt'; 'Munten van gravin Adela', Jaarboek voor Munt- en Penningkunde 67 (1980). The loss of a hand for false coin is Carolingian and English law (?)

stories.title: The son who was counted
stories.summary: Hathugard of the ale-house asks every boat about a boy given as a hostage in 785; he is the younger brother of Brunger, the mate. The trail runs from the ferry here to the palace at Noviomagus and up the Rhine road to Mogontia, where it ends about 805.
stories.picture: Inside a low Saxon ale-house by firelight: a tall grey-fair woman with a ladle stands over a seated merchant, asking; behind her, half in shadow, a big fair man with a seax looks at the floor.

beats.text: Hathugard asks her question before she pours. If the merchant promises to ask along the Rhine, she tells what she knows: thirteen years old, a scar through the left eyebrow from a calf's kick, answers to Brunric.

Thancric, once he trusts the merchant, says what he never told her in full: the hostages were handed on the west bank to the palace's men from Noviomagus, and the tally named the lord each boy was meant for. This is the trail (sets sx_brother_trail).
Carrying for the host shows the merchant how it is done: the same count's men who buy the oats lead the new hostages west in autumn. Brunger will not row that week.
At the palace a clerk can be brought to look at the old tally, for a gift or a service: the boys of that district went to a bishop's household on the middle Rhine.
On the Rhine road every bishop and abbot has Saxon hostages at his table or in his fields. Somebody remembers a boy with a split eyebrow going on upriver.
The trail ends at Mogontia: a man of thirty-three with a Frankish haircut and a split eyebrow, who has not heard his own tongue spoken kindly in twenty years (sets sx_brother_found).
Whatever was found is brought home to the ale-house, and Hathugard pours first for once.
The king's huntsman, a Saxon carried west, sends word by any boat bound for the IJssel: tell the ale-wife the man from the king's wood is alive.

endings.how: The brother was found at Mogontia and brought down the river before 806, by leave of his lord or without it.
endings.text: Brunric sits at his mother's hearth and speaks Saxon like a child of thirteen. If he came without leave the king's men may ask for him (sx_carried_fugitive), and the ale-house has a new door at the back.
endings.reward: Brunger is the house's man for life and will not leave at any venture's end; Hathugard is a fast friend; free lodging and winter stores at Daventre; a second strong oar who knows the Rhine road.

endings.how: The brother was found and would not come: he has a wife, a lord and a place.
endings.text: The merchant brings his word and a lock of his hair. Hathugard hears it standing, thanks him, and brews. Brunger says nothing for a month and then says one proverb.
endings.reward: Brunger stays; Hathugard is friendly; she tells the merchant where her husband buried what the family saved from the Weser, and it is his to fetch for a half share.

endings.how: The merchant promised and never asked, or the years ran out with Hathugard's life in 806.
endings.text: She dies at Martinmas with the question unanswered. Brunger buries her in the churchyard, south of the church, and leaves the boat at the next landing where there are Saxons.
endings.reward: Nothing; the mate's seat is empty and Saxons on this river hear why.

endings.how: The merchant told the count's men what the ferryman sees at night.
endings.text: Thancric loses the crossing and a Frank poles the ferry. The count is pleased. Nobody on the bank will sell the merchant ale.
endings.reward: The count's favour and a season's carrying for the host at a good price; every Saxon at Daventre is wary from then on.

stories.reward: A crewman bound to the house, a hearth at Daventre that is always open, and the knowledge of the Rhine road's great households.

stories.title: North of the grave, south of the grave
stories.summary: Saxon converts and Frankish soldiers hear the same Mass over Lebuin's grave, and the priest Liudbod wants a bell to call them with instead of a soldier's shout. Meanwhile somebody is leaving offerings on the Heest, and the merchant sees who.
stories.picture: The dark inside of a plank church: one lamp over a stone slab in the floor, armed Franks standing on the left of it, bare-headed Saxons on the right, a small priest between them lifting a hand bell.

beats.text: At Mass the merchant has to choose a side of the grave to stand on, and both sides notice. Liudbod asks him afterwards to carry a letter to the bishop at Traiectum: the rope is ready, send the bell.
Going up the Heest for a look at the river, the merchant finds the hollow, the crock and the rags, and on a second visit a woman from the south side of the church putting down honey.
Bishop Hamacar has no bell to spare, but there is bronze to be had if someone will pay for the founding, or carry an old cracked bell up from Dorestad.
Liudger rides through on his way to the western Saxons and lodges with Liudbod. He asks the merchant, before he tells him anything, what he saw on the hill.
On the Frisian shore the same question is being settled the hard way: shrines broken, treasure taken. People there ask what the priest at Daventre does about his hill, and whether it works.
The bishop's answer comes back up the river: no bell to spare, but bronze, if someone pays the founder. Whoever pays hears it rung over both sides of the grave.
On Lebuin's day, the morrow of Martinmas, both sides of the grave sing the same thing, and a few of them in the same time. After it the river goes round the town on both sides until spring.

endings.how: The merchant paid for the bell or carried one up the river, and kept quiet about the Heest.
endings.text: The bell hangs in a frame by the church door. The Saxons come when it rings, a little late, and the soldiers are told to leave their shouting at the ferry. The offerings on the hill grow fewer on their own, or are better hidden.
endings.reward: The work daventre.work.bell done; Liudbod a fast friend who reads and writes letters for the house free; the house's dead remembered at Lebuin's feast.

endings.how: The merchant told Liudger or the priest who goes up the hill.
endings.text: Liudger has the hollow filled and a cross set on the Heest. The woman does penance in the churchyard for three Sundays. The Saxon side of the church looks at the merchant and then does not.
endings.reward: Liudger's goodwill at Emuthon, Doccinga and Traiectum, and a letter that opens church doors on the Frisian shore; Saxons at Daventre are cool, and Hathugard waters the ale for a year.

endings.how: The merchant left something on the hill himself.
endings.text: Nobody says anything. Brunger rows as if the boat were lighter. If the priest hears, it is a matter for confession and a fine in wax.
endings.reward: Brunger's and the Saxons' trust (a better price for honey, horses and hides from across the border); a risk that a king's man or a priest learns of it later.

stories.reward: A bell with the house's gift remembered at it, or a missionary's letter, or the border's trust: which one says what kind of house this is.

stories.title: Old names on new plots
stories.summary: When the river leaves Dorestad the trade goes up the IJssel, and Thiadlef pegs out a street on the bank with a string. The house can take the plot beside his, lose it in the fire of 882, and help raise the wall that keeps the next fleet out.
stories.picture: A river bank at low sun: a thin man in a worn blue cloak kneels to drive a peg, a knotted string running from his hand along a row of half-built timber houses; a wooden church on its dune behind, a barge unloading.

beats.text: Thiadlef offers the plot beside his own to a house that had a jetty at Dorestad, before the bishop's steward sells it to a stranger. Three hundred pennies, and the ground must be raised with sods against the flood.
Word that the abbot of Saint-Bertin has had his seven manses in the port confirmed by King Charles. A cellarer's man from the far west is asking who will carry the abbey's wine and wool.
The great army winters in the palace. Anyone who lies there can count the ships and bring the count up the IJssel before the ships come.
Late in the year the Northmen burn the port where Saint Lebuin rests and kill many. A house that was warned has its goods across the river on the Worp; a house that was not has a plot of ash.
The bishop calls every plot-holder to a stretch of wall: sods, stakes and a ditch, nearly two kilometres. A house can dig its own stretch or pay for it.
King Zwentibold rules that the church's men here have the freedom they had at Dorestad. A house that holds its plot of the bishop is the church's man.

endings.how: The house took a plot before 882, stayed after the fire and built or paid for its stretch of the wall.
endings.text: The house is a Daventre house, with a name on the bank, a stretch of wall called after it and the bishop's freedom from the king's toll. Thiadlef's sons call the merchant's heir cousin, which is not true and is meant kindly.
endings.reward: unlock_plot_daventre, the work daventre.work.wall_share, and from 896 unlock_charter_daventre; the house may make Daventre its home port (the spine's df_moved).

endings.how: The house took a plot and was not there, or not warned, in 882.
endings.text: The plot is a black rectangle with four pegs in it. Thiadlef, carrying sods, says only that Dorestad went the same way and took longer over it.
endings.reward: The plot is still the house's, bare; whatever was stored on it is lost; the heir may rebuild at half cost because the name is known.

endings.how: The house would not peg ground on a border river and went to Tiel, Traiectum or over the sea.
endings.text: Other names fill the bank. The house is a guest at Daventre like anyone else and pays the king's toll from 896.
endings.reward: Nothing here; the silver is saved for another river.

stories.reward: A home on the IJssel that outlives Dorestad: a plot, a stretch of wall, the church's freedom from the toll.

stories.title: The bishop's swallow
stories.summary: Bishop Radboud lives in exile by Lebuin's church, writes the saint's Life and a poem about a swallow, and wants news of Utrecht more than he wants silver. A merchant who is his eyes on the river is repaid in the only coin a bishop in exile has: letters, and a name in the right book.
stories.picture: A timber doorway in morning light: a thin tonsured man with inky fingers sits on the threshold with a wax tablet on his knee, looking up at a swallow's nest under the eave; a merchant stands in the yard with his cap in his hand.

beats.text: Radboud asks what the river is doing: who holds the mouths, whether Saint Martin's at Traiectum has a roof. He wants a true account, each spring, from someone who has been there.
The fort at Traiectum is half ruin, with a priest or two holding on. They give the merchant a stone from Saint Martin's altar step to carry up the IJssel, wrapped in a cloth.
Radboud needs parchment and a book to copy from for his Life of Lebuin. Parchment is to be had on the Rhine; a book is dearer than the boat.
On the feast of Saint Andrew's eve word comes from Ootmarsum: the bishop is dead. He is carried here and buried in the north part of the church, and the clerks ask who will pay for the lamp.

endings.how: The merchant brought true word of Traiectum each spring and the altar stone with it.
endings.text: Radboud sets the stone under Lebuin's altar and has the merchant's name written in the church's book of the living. When Balderic takes the see home about 920, the house's name goes with the book.
endings.reward: The bishop's letter of protection (a church's man free of the king's toll at Daventre and, from 920, known at Traiectum); the house's names prayed for; a clerk who reads and writes for the house at no charge.

endings.how: The merchant supplied parchment and lent or found a book.
endings.text: The Life of Lebuin is written on skins the house carried. Radboud lets the merchant's reader copy what he likes from the bishop's chest.
endings.reward: Leave to copy texts at Daventre (act copy_text free at the bishop's house and later at Traiectum); a standing order for parchment at a good price.

endings.how: The merchant did little while he lived, and paid for the lamp over his grave.
endings.text: A lamp burns in the north part of the church. Balderic's clerks note who paid for it, without warmth and without forgetting.
endings.reward: A fair hearing from Bishop Balderic; alms counted to the house's name.

stories.reward: A bishop's protection and the house's name in a book that goes home to Utrecht.

stories.title: The Hand and the cross
stories.summary: About the year 1000 Deventer strikes the pennies that pay for the north's furs and wax, and a countess copies the English king's Hand on to a penny of her own. The moneyer Hrotmar wants to know where his coins end up, and will pay for English silver and for an answer.
stories.picture: A dim mint with one door: a stocky man in a leather apron holds a die in his fist over a block, hammer raised; in a wooden bowl beside him pale new pennies, the top one showing a hand coming down out of a cloud.

beats.text: Hrotmar changes the merchant's silver and asks a favour: bring English pennies with the Hand on them, unclipped, for the die-cutter to look at. He pays weight for weight, less a little.
The English king's Hand pennies are everywhere, and so are the fleets they are paid to. A moneyer by the river wants to know who on the continent is copying his king.
A die turns up that is not the king's: the Hand on one side, Deventer's cross on the other, struck for Countess Adela. Hrotmar says nothing against it and weighs one very carefully.
In the north a Deventer penny is taken by weight, cut in half for small change and pecked with a knife to see if it is silver. A trader shows one with the king's name sliced through.
The king's own mint now strikes the Hand. Hrotmar has what he wanted: an answer, brought back by someone who followed the coin.

endings.how: The merchant brought Hand pennies from England and the tale of a cut Deventer penny from the north.
endings.text: Hrotmar keeps the halved penny on a nail over his block. He changes the house's silver first and at the best rate he is allowed.
endings.reward: The best exchange at Daventre's mint for the house and its heirs; the knowledge that Deventer pennies pass by weight across the north (a price word for furs and wax).

endings.how: The merchant carried the countess's pennies and spoke for them abroad.
endings.text: Adela's Hand penny goes north in the house's chest and is taken as readily as the king's. The countess remembers her friends, and so, later, do her enemies.
endings.reward: A lady's favour in Hamaland and a standing order for English silver; the king's men and the bishop are cool toward the house while she is at war with her neighbours.

endings.how: The merchant told the king's men that a coin not the king's was being struck.
endings.text: Nothing happens to the countess; she is too great. Hrotmar is questioned for a week and counts his fingers afterwards. The king's mint copies her coin anyway.
endings.reward: A small reward in silver from the king's man; the moneyer changes the house's silver last and at the worst rate he is allowed.

stories.reward: A mint that favours the house, and the knowledge of where Frankish silver goes when it leaves the river.

works.name: A bell for Lebuin's church
works.what: A bronze bell hung in a timber frame by the church door, so that the border is called to Mass by a bell and not by a soldier. The priest has had the rope ready for years.
works.needs: The priest or the bishop easy with the house; bronze founded at Traiectum or an old bell carried up from Dorestad.
works.gives: The house's gift is remembered at every Mass: standing with churchmen in the whole region, Saxons at Daventre a little warmer, and the story 'North of the grave, south of the grave' can end with the bell. Lost in the fire of 882 unless carried over the river.
works.picture: A small bronze bell in a frame of four posts beside a plank church door, a rope hanging from it, Saxons and Franks coming up the dune from two sides.
works.source: works_793.json, bell. Liudger's want of 'priests, books and a bell' is the spine's (cast.liudger); no bell is recorded here

works.name: A share in the weirs at the brook mouth
works.what: A third of the stake fences and basket traps across the mouth of the brook, with the smoking rack that goes with them. The fishers mend the weir; the sharers take a third of the eels.
works.needs: A fisher of the bank willing to sell a share, so some good dealing here first.
works.gives: Smoked eels each autumn to sell or to provision the boat with, without buying; a reason for the fishers to tell the house what the river is doing.
works.picture: Two wattle fences across a brook mouth under alders, basket traps in the gaps, eels on a rack over a low fire.
works.source: works_793.json, fish_weir. The settlement was a fishing and trading place (dossier 1); the weirs are invented

works.name: A plot on the bank
works.what: A strip of the sand ridge, end on to the river, pegged out with a string and raised with sods against the flood. Room for a house, a pit and a boat path.
works.needs: Bought of the bishop's steward; a house that had a plot at Dorestad is offered one first.
works.gives: The house may store goods, winter and build at Daventre; from 896 a plot-holder under the bishop is the church's man at the toll. The same as unlock_plot_daventre.
works.picture: Four pegs and a string on a sandy ridge between two timber houses, a pile of cut sods, the river below.
works.source: unlocks_793.json, unlock_plot_daventre (300 d, from 850); works_793.json, plot; dossier 2 on the raised ground

works.name: A storehouse on the plot
works.what: A timber storehouse with a raised floor on the house's own plot, a door toward the bank and a pit lined with wattle for casks.
works.gives: Goods kept here from one season to the next, so the house can buy before the host comes in spring and sell when it has come. Burned in 882 unless the house was warned.
works.picture: A plank storehouse on short posts at the river end of a plot, its door open on stacked sacks and casks, a barge below.
works.source: works_793.json, storehouse; the burn layer of 882: Canon van Deventer, 'Verdedigingswal'

works.name: Your stretch of the wall
works.what: A measured length of the earth wall raised after the fire: sods cut and stacked, oak stakes along the top, the ditch dug at its foot. Every plot-holder owes a stretch; a house can pay others to dig its own.
works.needs: A plot on the bank, held through the fire of 882.
works.gives: The stretch is called after the house; the bishop and the plot-holders count the house as one of the town; goods stored at Daventre are safe from the next fleet up the river.
works.picture: Men and women with baskets of sods on a half-raised earth bank, a row of split-oak stakes going in along the top, black burned ground showing in the cut.
works.source: works_793.json, wall_share; Canon van Deventer, 'Verdedigingswal' (1.9 km, finished before 890). That plot-holders each owed a stretch is the game's (?)

ships.note: The fishers' boat of the weirs and the brooks: an oak log hollowed with fire and adze. Cheap, and good for nothing wider than the river.
ships.picture: A dugout tied to a weir stake, a basket of eels in it.

ships.note: A small plank boat for errands across to the Worp and up the brooks.
ships.picture: A flat little plank boat drawn up on the bank beside the ferry post.

ships.how: bought second-hand, or built to order in a season
ships.note: The cheapest hull that will carry a cargo between Daventre, Traiectum and Dorestad: a widened log with planks added, hauled upstream from the bank.
ships.picture: A long narrow river freighter on a log keel, a towing mast forward, three men and a load of sacks.
ships.source: unlocks_793.json, unlock_ship_logboat_expanded (250 d at Daventre); ship_classes_793.json

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: Flat-bottomed, oak, pegged with wood and caulked with moss: the barge of this river, as the ones found in its quay. From about 950 the oak comes from the Ardennes. It will never see the sea.
ships.picture: A broad flat barge on rollers in a cut in the bank, half planked, a wright driving moss into a seam.
ships.source: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, MaSS, Deventer 1 (990), 2 (about 1035), 3 (after about 913); Design/content/ships.md

ships.how: hired with its crew from the bishop's steward
ships.note: The bishop in exile keeps a river ship for his own journeys and his estates' renders; in a quiet month his steward hires it out.
ships.picture: A river ship with eight oars and an awning aft, a cross on a pole at the bow, moored below the church.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json, river_estate_ship; the bishops' house here about 857 to 920 (dossier 2). That it was hired out is the game's (?)

sayings.text: When Franks buy oats in spring, bury your honey.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the host bought up stores each May (spine, saxon_end)

sayings.text: A baptised wolf still knows the wood.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on the forced baptisms of 785 (Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 8)

sayings.text: I forsake the devil, and all the devil's works and words: Thunaer and Woden and Saxnote, and all the fiends that are their fellows.
sayings.source: the Old Saxon baptismal vow, late 8th century (texts_793.json saxon_vow); our own rendering from the Old Saxon. Said here flatly, by people who were made to say it

sayings.text: Three times built, twice burned: the saint is ahead by one.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Lebuin's church (dossier 2); after 882 they say 'four times built'

sayings.text: A Frank's wergild is three free men's. The Franks wrote the law.
sayings.source: a proverb turned, invented, on the Ewa ad Amorem, about 802-803: a Frankish man 600 solidi, a freeman 200 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Francorum_Chamavorum)

sayings.text: The river asks nobody's faith. It drowns both kinds.
The Frisian's cloak is short so that he can run back to his boat.
sayings.source: a Frank's joke, invented, after Notker's story of the emperor and the short Frisian cloaks (Gesta Karoli I.34; Grant 1907), not quoted

sayings.text: At Dorestad the river left us. Here it only floods us.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; said after 863

sayings.text: A monk of Saint-Amand has praised bald men in a poem where every word begins with C. Our bishop says it is the cleverest waste of a winter he ever read.
sayings.source: a churchman's joke, invented, said after 900: Hucbald of Saint-Amand's Ecloga de calvis, 146 lines, every word beginning with C; Hucbald also wrote a Life of Lebuin, 918-930 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hucbald)

sayings.text: A penny has two faces and no opinions.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; said after 990

easter_eggs.text: The posts of the church's south wall stand a stride further out than they should. Liudger had built the wall before he found the grave under it, and moved the wall rather than the saint.
easter_eggs.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.15; Vita Lebuini antiqua; told in our own words

easter_eggs.text: Old people in the town say the saint did not die by a Saxon's hand at all: he died of the cold, in the lane that goes down to the bank.
easter_eggs.source: Canon van Deventer, 'Lebuinus': the town tradition that he died of the cold in the Assenstraat. How old the tradition is, is not known (?)

easter_eggs.text: After about 820 the church shows an ivory cup as Lebuin's own chalice. It was carved at the emperor's court a generation after he died. Nobody at Daventre has done the sum.
easter_eggs.source: Canon van Deventer, 'Lebuinus': the 'Lebuin chalice' is an ivory cup of the early 9th century from the Aachen court school

easter_eggs.text: In the facing of the quay, about the year 1000, there are planks with old peg holes and moss still in the seams: a barge whose oak was felled in the spring of 990, sailing nowhere now.
easter_eggs.source: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, MaSS, Deventer 1

easter_eggs.text: Where the wall is cut, a black band a hand deep runs under the grass. The children dig charred grain out of it.
easter_eggs.source: Canon van Deventer, 'Verdedigingswal': a burn layer 20 cm thick under the wall. The grain is invented

easter_eggs.text: A Northman in a far harbour shows a penny he was paid in the islands at the edge of the world. It reads, in three lines, the name of this town.
easter_eggs.source: A Deventer coin lay in the Sandur hoard on the Faroes (de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deventer); the legend DAVNER/A: Künker

easter_eggs.text: The Frisians on the bank say Taventeri. The Franks write Daventre. The Saxons say it in a way no clerk has tried to spell.
easter_eggs.source: Annales Fuldenses 882: 'the port called Taventeri in the Frisian tongue'; Saint-Bertin 877: 'in Daventre portu'. The Saxon form is not recorded

easter_eggs.text: The Worp, across the river, is the best building ground in sight, and nobody has ever built on it. Ask why and you are told the river wants it back each winter.
easter_eggs.source: dossier 1: the low open Worp on the far bank, never built on. The reason is the game's

unlocks.what: A hearth at Daventre: Hathugard's bench is the house's whenever the boat lies here.
unlocks.how: Promise to ask after her son along the Rhine, and bring any word at all before 806 (the story 'The son who was counted').
unlocks.gives: Free lodging and winter quarters at Daventre while she lives; rumours of the border a season early; npc alewife feeling up.

unlocks.what: The IJssel by heart: the bars, the wading place, the winter channel round the north-east.
unlocks.how: Be friendly with Thancric the ferryman and cross with him at low water three times, or keep Brunger as mate for three years.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_pilot_ijssel: no pilot needed and no grounding at low water between the Rhine and Daventre.

unlocks.what: A plot on the bank at Daventre.
unlocks.how: From 850, 300 pennies to the bishop's steward; offered first to a house that had a plot at Dorestad (the story 'Old names on new plots').
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_plot_daventre: store, winter and build here; Daventre may become the house's home after Dorestad.

unlocks.what: A stretch of the wall called by the house's name.
unlocks.how: Hold a plot through the fire of 882 and dig or pay for the stretch between 883 and 889.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_work_daventre_wall_share: goods stored at Daventre are safe from fleets; standing with the bishop and the town.

unlocks.what: The church's freedom from the king's toll at Daventre, as it was at Dorestad.
unlocks.how: Be the church's man (hold a plot of the bishop, or carry Bishop Radboud's letter) when King Zwentibold's ruling comes in 896; set by the card long.tiel.dorestads_freedom.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_charter_daventre: 'Show the charter' at the toll does toll none here. Lapses with the grant of 1046 unless the bishop renews it.

unlocks.how: Bring him true word of Traiectum each spring, 900 to 917, and the stone from Saint Martin's altar step (the story 'The bishop's swallow').
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_title_radbouds_man: a church's man at Daventre and, from 920, at Traiectum; leave to copy texts at the bishop's house.

unlocks.what: First place and the best rate at the mint.
unlocks.how: Bring Hrotmar English Hand pennies and word of where his own coins go (the story 'The Hand and the cross'), 990 to 1024.
unlocks.gives: The smallest loss the law allows on changing silver at Daventre, for the house and its heirs.

unlocks.how: Buy from the forge three times and pay on the day, or bring him word of his son from the host.
unlocks.gives: Rivets at 13 d a keg against the table's 16, and bar iron a penny under the market, while he lives.

unlocks.what: The moneyer's thanks for word of where his pennies go
unlocks.how: Between 990 and 1024, knowing the northern reckoning (flag sv_scale or rf_two_weights), tell Hrotmar how his pennies are weighed, cut and pecked in the north (the card harbour.hand_and_cross.daventre).
unlocks.gives: flag rf_hrotmar_friend: twenty pennies at once, and the first step of the unlock daventre.mint_friend
